name: Software as a Medical Device
title: Software as a Medical Device
answer: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device. It includes diagnostic support, treatment planning, patient monitoring, and image analysis tools that run on general purpose hardware. The category excludes software that merely manages administrative or billing data. A working professional should understand that regulatory status depends on intended use, not on the technology itself.

sections.body: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device. It includes diagnostic support, treatment planning, patient monitoring, and image analysis tools that run on general purpose hardware. The category excludes software that merely manages administrative or billing data. A working professional should understand that regulatory status depends on intended use, not on the technology itself.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: SaMD typically runs on hospital servers, cloud platforms, or dedicated workstations, often integrated with picture archiving and communication systems and electronic health records. It may also operate on mobile devices or embedded within clinical workflows through application programming interfaces. The infrastructure must support version control, audit logging, and controlled updates because a change to the software can alter its medical function. Network segmentation and access controls are common because these tools handle patient data and connect to clinical systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a defined software development lifecycle that includes requirements specification, risk management, verification, validation, and clinical evaluation. Manufacturers classify the software by risk using frameworks such as the International Medical Device Regulators Forum categories, which range from non-serious to critical situations. Clinical evidence is gathered through analytical studies, bench testing, and sometimes clinical trials, depending on the risk class. Post-market monitoring collects real world performance data and adverse events to confirm that the software continues to meet its intended use.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on regulatory approval, cybersecurity obligations, and liability for harm. Regulators such as the US Food and Drug Administration and European notified bodies require documentation of the software's development history, data sources, and change control. Patients and clinicians have rights to understand the basis of a software's output, and manufacturers carry responsibility for defects that cause injury. Provenance of training data and clinical validation data is increasingly examined in product liability and wrongful death litigation, as tracked in this site's compliance and regulation pages.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more frequent software updates, including adaptive algorithms that learn from new data after deployment. Regulators are developing frameworks for predetermined change control plans that allow certain modifications without a new submission. Greater emphasis on real world evidence and interoperability will likely shape how SaMD is validated across different populations and clinical settings. The growth of medical AI models tracked on this site suggests that governance will need to keep pace with both the number of tools and the complexity of their updates.
